scenarios.title: Receive the goalie’s released outlet
scenarios.objective: Prepare a receiver and next option after a stated goalie outlet.
scenarios.briefing: The Navy goalie has just released a short pass toward YOU near the puck-side corner. The puck is shown loose in transit. Gold 1 is approaching that side; D2 waits across the net and C is inside. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.

questions.prompt: Why is the puck not assigned to YOU yet?

options.text: C has settled it at centre ice
The outlet is still in transit
The goalie has already covered it again

questions.explanation: The briefing identifies a released pass and the marker remains loose between goalie and receiver.

questions.prompt: Select two receiver checks before the pass arrives.

options.text: Gold 1’s approach
An assumption that the corner will stay unpressured
The next outlet toward C or D2

questions.explanation: Preparing a next option is useful only while pressure and the reception permit it.

questions.prompt: Arrange one outlet reception routine.

options.text: Scan the approaching forechecker
Prepare to receive the goalie’s pass
Control or redirect according to the actual lane

questions.explanation: One-touch play may be possible, but this routine does not require it.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a ready receiving angle near the corner.
questions.explanation: The example meets the short pass with a view toward inside support. The pass travel and stick technique are not simulated.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 reaches your planned next lane before reception. What is sensible?

options.text: Send the puck along that lane automatically
Assume the goalie can recall the pass
Reassess protection or another outlet

questions.explanation: The reception plan should change with a closing opponent.

questions.prompt: What could YOU communicate to help the goalie before the next retrieval?
questions.explanation: Describe a clear readiness or pressure message tied to this side, rather than a vague demand for the puck.

questions.prompt: What should YOU tell the goalie before the outlet?

options.text: I am showing a lane; call if Gold 1 closes it
The pass is already received
The corner is open for sure

questions.explanation: The call gives the goalie a named receiver and a conditional lane.

questions.prompt: Which two checks belong before receiving?

options.text: Gold 1's route
D2 or C's support position
The loose puck guarantees a clean first touch

questions.explanation: Pressure and support shape the reception; the goalie release does not guarantee control.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a receiving angle near the corner with the goalie visible.
questions.explanation: This point offers a changed receiving lane without assuming the puck arrives.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 reaches your planned lane first. What should you communicate?
questions.explanation: Call the changed pressure, show another support lane, and let the goalie know the first receiver is covered.

questions.prompt: What has Gold 1 explicitly changed?

options.text: Moved into the direct pass connection
Joined Navy as a receiver
Left the rush entirely

questions.explanation: The briefing identifies the defender’s lane adjustment; it does not state a guaranteed shot.

questions.prompt: Which two cues belong in your next choice?

options.text: The rule that every two-on-one must end in a pass
The goalie and F2’s availability
Gold 1’s lane and reach

questions.explanation: A numerical advantage still requires comparing actual options.

questions.prompt: Arrange one read after the lane changes.

options.text: Update Gold 1’s position
Compare shot, pass and carry possibilities
Choose an available play before pressure changes again

questions.explanation: The sequence teaches comparison, not an automatic pass or shot.

questions.prompt: Move YOU forward to compare another carrier angle.
questions.explanation: The reference changes both net and pass angles. It does not establish that YOU can reach it before Gold 1 or B reacts.

questions.prompt: If Gold 1 turns fully toward YOU and F2’s route clears, what might improve?

options.text: A need to ignore the goalie
A checked passing option to F2
A claim that F2 remains covered exactly as before

questions.explanation: The pass may become more useful, but reception and interception must still be assessed.

questions.prompt: How can a suggested answer acknowledge both a possible shot and a possible pass?
questions.explanation: Explain which visible or stated cue favours each instead of claiming the source mandates one outcome.

questions.prompt: What should YOU say as Gold 1 changes the lane?

options.text: F2 is available if the defender commits; I will keep the puck protected
Choose a shot before comparing F2’s route
F2 owns the puck

questions.explanation: The call connects defender commitment to the cross-ice option without forcing it.

questions.prompt: Which two cues support the second option?

options.text: Gold 1 turns toward YOU
F2 has a reachable route
The net location alone

questions.explanation: Defender commitment and receiver access make the second option useful.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a carrier angle that keeps F2 across the ice.
questions.explanation: This point changes the carrier line while preserving F2 in view.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 stays between you and F2. Explain the safer branch.
questions.explanation: Protect the puck and keep scanning for a carry or another lane; a cross-ice pass needs real access.

scenarios.title: Support the second touch of a wall battle
scenarios.objective: Distinguish first pressure from a second-player recovery role.
scenarios.briefing: F1 and Gold 1 contest the puck near the side boards. YOU are the second Navy player. C stays inside as an outlet. The drill asks YOU to read the next loose touch rather than occupy F1’s exact spot. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: F1 is identified in the wall contest; YOU have the second-player role.

questions.prompt: Which Navy player is assigned the first wall contest?

options.text: C
D1
F1

questions.explanation: F1 is identified in the wall contest; YOU have the second-player role.

questions.prompt: Choose two things that can make second support useful.

options.text: A read of the next loose touch
Separation from the first contest
Standing on F1’s position to add another label

questions.explanation: A second role should complement the first player and the outlet, not merely duplicate them.

questions.prompt: Order one second-support read.

options.text: Watch the contest and puck direction
Check C and the opposing support
Move to the next useful touch or containment position

questions.explanation: The direction of the next touch determines the action; the static puck does not predict the winner.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than the battle to illustrate a second-touch support pocket.
questions.explanation: This reference separates YOU from F1 and leaves a possible connection to C. Different bounces require different positions.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 moves onto C’s outlet. Which two checks help you adjust?

options.text: Look for the next available pass if Navy wins the puck
Recheck whether C can still receive safely
Assume F1 has won the puck because Gold 2 moved

questions.explanation: Winning the battle does not guarantee the originally planned outlet.

questions.prompt: Explain a useful second-player job if F1 does not win the puck cleanly.
questions.explanation: Contain an exit, collect a loose touch or support defensive recovery; tie the answer to Gold 1, Gold 2 and C.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate in the wall battle?

options.text: I am above the battle; call if the outlet lane changes
The second touch belongs to whoever arrives first
C remains the outlet even when Gold closes that lane

questions.explanation: The message names a support relationship and keeps the outlet dependent on the battle.

questions.prompt: Which two events change second support?

options.text: Gold 2 closes C
F1 wins the puck cleanly
The wall battle remains below

questions.explanation: Coverage and possession determine the next support job.

questions.prompt: Move YOU closer to Navy’s net than the battle while keeping C visible.
questions.explanation: This example is on the navy-net side of the wall contest and separate from F1, with C inside as another outlet. Reposition again if the loose puck or Gold pressure changes.

questions.prompt: Gold 2 moves onto C’s outlet. What should you adjust?
questions.explanation: Name the covered outlet, keep the net-side support, and check whether F1 or another lane becomes reachable.

scenarios.title: Protect possession while a teammate changes
scenarios.objective: Make a conditional puck-management choice during a stated substitution.
scenarios.briefing: F3 is changing at the bench and is unavailable for the next few moments. YOU hold the puck in the neutral zone. D2 is behind YOU; F1 and F2 are farther ahead. This is a possession exercise, not a too-many-players rules test. Navy attacks Gold’s net and defends Navy’s net. This is a selected-player teaching view; no movement is implied unless stated.
cues: The briefing states F3 is unavailable; the scenario does not draw or count a player entering the ice.

questions.prompt: Which two checks matter while support is reduced?

A belief that every change requires a blind dump
Whether D2 offers a controlled reset

questions.prompt: Arrange one read during this change.

options.text: Confirm available teammates
Assess pressure and controlled options
Choose a play and communicate the next support need

questions.explanation: This is a stated game-management situation, not a substitution-rule sequence.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to compare a position preserving a connection to D2.
questions.explanation: A modest retreat may maintain a reset while support changes. A forward option may still be preferable if clearly available.

questions.prompt: The new F3 arrives in a clear middle lane. What can you reconsider?

options.text: The idea that support remains reduced forever
A requirement to use D2 despite the new option
Whether a new forward connection has appeared

questions.explanation: The availability change should update the picture instead of locking in the earlier conservative plan.

questions.prompt: Why is “a teammate is changing” not enough information to demand a dump-in?
questions.explanation: Explain how pressure, control and other teammates could support a carry, pass or reset.

questions.prompt: What should YOU call during the line change?

options.text: D2 is my support; I am protecting the puck-side lane
The reduced support makes a forward option unusable by itself
F1 has stopped playing

questions.explanation: The call keeps possession protection tied to D2 and the visible pressure.

questions.prompt: Which two cues decide a safe hold?

options.text: Gold 1 closes the middle
D2 remains reachable
A teammate is changing somewhere on the bench

questions.explanation: Pressure and support determine whether holding helps maintain possession.

questions.prompt: Move YOU to a position connected to D2 while protecting the puck side.
questions.explanation: This point changes the carrier relationship and keeps D2 visible.

questions.prompt: F3 arrives in a clear middle lane. What can you reconsider?
questions.explanation: Recheck the middle connection before dumping. If Gold closes it again, return to puck protection and D2 support.

questions.prompt: What should YOU communicate from low support?

options.text: I am low support; check whether the slot lane opens
The slot is always covered
F1 stays the low outlet even when the carrier angle changes

questions.prompt: Which two cues affect low support?

options.text: Gold 1 leaves the slot route
F2 remains a reachable outlet
The low area fixes every next pass

questions.prompt: Move YOU off the puck-side half wall toward a new low-support angle.

questions.prompt: Gold 1 pressures YOU on the wall. What should be checked?
